leads.title: Oracle against Babylon; the Day of YHWH darkens the heavens ↔ Those sent forth: the refrain of woe
leads.summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 same element.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/08-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Stars and constellations (kesilim) give no light, the sun is dark at its rising and the moon does not shine (weight 6.8). Pair score 6.8.

Only in Oracle against Babylon; the Day of YHWH darkens the heavens: Babylon, glory of kingdoms, will be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah; Wordplay: the Day comes 'like destruction (shod) from Shaddai'; God makes the heavens tremble and the earth shake from its place on the day of his wrath; God makes mortals rarer than fine gold, humans than the gold of Ophir; God stirs up the Medes, who care nothing for silver or gold; God musters his consecrated ones and mighty men; a host from the end of heaven, the weapons of his wrath; The quake of the Hour: every nursing mother forgets her suckling, every pregnant one miscarries, people seem drunk though not drunk; Ruined city never reinhabited, even by Arab tents or shepherds; inhabited by desert creatures, ostriches, jackals and dancing goat-demons (se'irim); The people's terror is like the pangs of a woman in labor with her first child; Oracle headed 'massa' (burden) against a named nation or place; The Day of YHWH: a coming day of divine judgment, terror and darkness; Brief oracles against neighboring nations (Amalek, Kenite, Asshur, Kittim).

Only in Those sent forth: the refrain of woe: Humans created from a despised fluid placed in a secure lodging (the womb) for a known term; On that day the damned do not speak and are not permitted to offer excuses; The earth is made a receptacle (kifat) that holds the living and the dead; Hell throws sparks as huge as castles, like yellow (or black) camels; The damned are led to a shadow of three branches that gives no shade nor protects from the flame; Every verse ends with the same response ('for his steadfast love is forever'), an antiphonal litany; In paradise the shades are close and the fruit clusters hang low within reach; Refrain 'Woe that day to the deniers' (waylun yawma'idhin lil-mukadhdhibin) repeated through a surah; At the end the sky is split, cleft or opened (infatarat, inshaqqat, furijat); At the end the mountains become a heap of running sand, are blown away, set in motion or turn into a mirage; God makes winds his messengers (angels) and flaming fire his ministers; God set the mountains as pegs or firm anchors (awtad, rawasi) for the earth; and 2 more.
